records.originHebrew: "וְאַחַר כָּךְ לִלְמֹד וּלְלַמֵּד" — אַחַר שֶׁקִּבֵּל מֵרַבּוֹתָיו, וְאַחַר כָּךְ מֵחֲבֵרָיו יוֹתֵר מֵהֶם (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב תַּעֲנִית דַּף ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳), זֶהוּ "לִלְמֹד" וּמִתַּלְמִידָיו יוֹתֵר מִכֻּלָּם — זֶהוּ "לְלַמֵּד" וְהֵם פָּרָשַׁת "וְאָהַבְתָּ" וּפָרָשַׁת "וְהָיָה [אִם שָׁמֹעַ]", כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת (דַּף י״ד עַמּוּד ב׳) אַחַר כָּךְ "וְלִשְׁמוֹר" — הוּא הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת קֹדֶם יְצִיאַת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לַפּוֹעַל, מִלְּשׁוֹן: "וְאָבִיו שָׁמַר [אֶת הַדָּבָר]", שֶׁהוּא לְשׁוֹן הַמְתָּנָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בַּעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת) שֶׁהַמִּצְוָה צְרִיכָה שְׁמִירָה וְהַמְתָּנָה לְהָכִין עַצְמוֹ, וּזְרִיזִין מַקְדִּימִין שֶׁמָּא יְקַדְּמֶנּוּ הַמָּוֶת וְזֶה כְּנֶגֶד "לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם", שֶׁאַחַר שֶׁעָבַר כָּל הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת הָאֵלֶּה, אָז יִהְיֶה מָתוּן, כִּי בָּטוּחַ "לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ" שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רִבּוּי בַּחַיִּים, וְלֹא יִפָּסֵק הַחֹשֶׁק מִמֶּנּוּ אַחַר זְמַן מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּהַתְחָלָה: כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לוֹ חֵשֶׁק, צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת זָרִיז לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ, שֶׁלֹּא יִפָּסֵק בֵּינְתַיִם הַחֵשֶׁק כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְנוּ בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר בְּעִנְיַן פֶּסַח מִצְרַיִם נֶאֱכַל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא הָלַךְ דֶּרֶךְ מַדְרֵגוֹת הַקּוֹדְמוֹת
records.originEnglish: Afterward, “to learn and to teach”: first one receives from his teachers, then still more from his colleagues, as is taught in Ta’anit 7a—this is “to learn”; and from his students more than from them all—this is “to teach.” These correspond to the passages “You shall love” and “And it shall be, if you listen,” as is taught in Berakhot 14b. Afterward, “to guard”: this is the reflection before an action comes into practice, from the expression “His father kept [the matter],” which signifies waiting. As is written in Asarah Ma’amarot, a mitzvah requires watchfulness and waiting so that one can prepare oneself, while the zealous act early lest death overtake them. This corresponds to “So that your days may be many.” After one has passed through all these levels, he should then be deliberate, for he is assured of “so that they may be many”: life will increase, and his desire will not cease after a time. At the beginning it is different. When a desire reaches him, he must act upon it promptly, lest the desire cease in the meantime. As we have written elsewhere concerning the Passover offering in Egypt, it is eaten in haste while one has not yet passed through the preceding levels.
records.themeTitle: From a fleeting awakening to deliberate service
records.themeSummary: Dover Tzedek reads the prayer’s stages as a change in spiritual readiness. A first desire can disappear and requires prompt action; established service allows preparation and patient deliberation.
records.targetHebrew: א] רֵאשִׁית כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּחִפָּזוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּפֶסַח מִצְרַיִם שֶׁהָיָה נֶאֱכָל בְּחִפָּזוֹן, וְלֹא פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת. מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה לְנַתֵּק עַצְמוֹ מִכָּל תַּאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא מְקֻשָּׁר בָּהֶם, צָרִיךְ לִשְׁמֹר הָרֶגַע שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם, וְלַחְפּוֹז עַל אוֹתוֹ רֶגַע לְמַהֵר לָצֵאת מֵהֶם, אוּלַי יוּכַל. וְאַחַר כָּךְ שׁוּב יֵלֵךְ בִּמְתִינוּת וּלְאַט, כְּדִין פֶּסַח דּוֹרוֹת.
records.targetEnglish: A person’s first entry into the service of God must be in haste, just as we find that the Passover offering in Egypt was eaten in haste, whereas the Passover offering of later generations was not. At the beginning, to detach oneself from all the desires of this world to which one is bound, one must guard the moment in which the desire for God awakens within, and rush upon that moment to hasten out of them, if perhaps one can. Afterward, one should again proceed with deliberation and slowly, like the law of the Passover offering of later generations.
records.explanation: Tzidkat HaTzadik states the distinction that explains Dover Tzedek’s apparently opposing counsels of waiting and haste. The first awakening must be protected because one is still bound to earlier desires; the later pace is deliberate. This is a precise development of the same Passover comparison, not a general instruction to rush every mitzvah or every religious impulse.
records.translationProvenance: English prepared for Akiva Publishing’s reviewed source and thematic collections. An identical target translation is retained from another reviewed record where indicated by the matching quotation. Hebrew quotations are unchanged canonical excerpts. Complete origin sections and complete target sections were read for these reciprocal connections; relevance and both directions were reviewed separately from the text hashes.
records.reverseThemeTitle: Haste at the beginning and deliberation afterward
records.reverseThemeSummary: The initial awakening must be seized before the desires that bind a person overwhelm it. After that first departure, service proceeds with a slower, deliberate pace.
records.reverseExplanation: Dover Tzedek locates this transition within the sequence “to learn, to teach, to guard, to do, and to establish.” It explains how patient preparation can become appropriate once the earlier stages have steadied the desire. This gives a fuller account of the deliberation with which Tzidkat HaTzadik concludes.

records.targetHebrew: היינו משום שבעומק הלב של ישראל נמצא יקרות גדול ועצום מאוד מה שאין נמצא כזאת בשום אומה ולשון וזאת היקרות ניכר מהכח המעצר שיש בהם לעצור ולצמצם לבל יחטפו לקבל שום דבר בחפזי מה שאין כח המעצר כזה גבי שום אומה ומזה בעצמו מוכח שיש בהם בקביעות כל מיני יקרות כי מי שיש לו הון רב ורכוש גדול אינו ממהר כ"כ לחטוף שום דבר בחפזון כי בטוח היטב ברכושו שיהיה בידו להשיג כל מגמת חפצו ומבוקשו בכל עת שיחפוץ כי רק האביון שמחוסר כל כאשר נזדמן לו דבר שחשקה נפשו אינו יכול לצמצם ולעצור א"ע מלחטוף אותה אצלו בחפזו כי מתירא אולי לא יהיה אח"כ לאל ידו להשיגה אבל מי שבטוח ברוב הינו ורכושו יכול שפיר לעצור עצמו ולהמתין בכל הטובות כדי שישיג אותם אח"כ ביתר שאת. ומביא הזוה"ק ראיה על זה הפירוש של מלת עצרת מהפסוק זה יעצור בעמי ולית עצור אלא מלכות וכו' כלומר מחמת עוצם בטוחות של המלך כי מי יש לו כ"כ בטוחות חזק ותקיפות כמו המלך שפורץ גדר לעשות לו דרך ואין מי שימחה בידו לזה יש נמי להמלך כח המעצור ביותר וגודל מתינות יותר מכל העם ולזה הוא באמת מלך על כל העם. וזהו זה יעצור בעמי ולית עצור אלא מלכות וכו':
records.targetEnglish: That is because in the depth of Israel’s heart there is a very great and immense preciousness, such as is not found in any other nation or language. This preciousness is evident in their power of restraint: they can hold themselves back and limit themselves so as not to snatch anything hastily, a power of restraint not found in any other nation. This itself demonstrates that every kind of preciousness is firmly established within them. Someone with abundant wealth and great possessions does not hurry so much to snatch something in haste, for he is secure in his possessions and knows that he will be able to obtain his desire and request whenever he wishes. Only the destitute person, who lacks everything, cannot hold himself back from snatching a desired thing when it happens to become available, because he fears that later it may no longer be within his power to obtain it. Someone secure in his abundant wealth and possessions can restrain himself and wait for every good thing, so as to obtain it afterward in greater measure. The Zohar brings proof for this interpretation of the word Atzeret from the verse “This one shall rule over My people”: “restraint signifies kingship.” That is, it comes from the king’s great confidence. Who possesses confidence and firmness like the king, who can break through a fence to make himself a path, with no one preventing him? He therefore also possesses the greatest power of restraint and greater deliberation than all the people, and is consequently truly king over the whole people. This is “This one shall rule over My people,” and “restraint signifies kingship.”
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim supplies the mechanism behind Dover Tzedek’s later deliberation: secure possession makes it possible to wait, while fear of losing the opportunity creates haste. In its Atzeret setting, restraint expresses inner wealth and kingship. Dover Tzedek applies a related distinction to the stability of the desire for service. The comparison concerns that stability; Sod Yesharim’s image of grabbing worldly goods does not negate the necessary initial haste described by Rav Tzadok.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Inner wealth makes patient restraint possible
records.reverseThemeSummary: Atzeret is read through the king’s power to restrain himself. Securely possessed inner worth allows a person to wait for good rather than grasp it as though it might immediately disappear.
records.reverseExplanation: Dover Tzedek applies the relation between confidence and patience to religious service itself. At first the desire is fragile and must be acted on promptly; after its earlier stages have been established, reflection and waiting become appropriate. This clarifies the spiritual significance of the secure wealth that allows restraint in Sod Yesharim.

records.originHebrew: וְאָמְרוּ שָׁם: ״מְנָא יָדְעָה?״ (בְּרָכוֹת י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳) כִּי קְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית מִדְּבָרִים שֶׁבְּצִנְעָה שֶׁאֵין נִיכָּר וְחַד אָמַר: ״שֶׁלֹּא רָאֲתָה זְבוּב עַל שֻׁלְחָנוֹ״ הַיְינוּ שֶׁהִכִּירָה בַּאֲכִילָתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּתַאֲוַת הַיֵּצֶר הַנִּמְשָׁל לִזְבוּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם ס״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳) וּמִזֶּה יָדְעָה שֶׁגָּדוּר בַּעֲרָיוֹת גַּם כֵּן וְחַד אָמַר: ״סָדִין שֶׁל פִּשְׁתָּן הִצִּיעָה לוֹ, וְלֹא רָאֲתָה קֶרִי עָלָיו״ אַף שֶׁטּוֹרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ מֵבִיא לִידֵי קֶרִי גַּם לַחֲסִידִים פְּעָמִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת (קכ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳) וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְהִזָּהֵר בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יֶאֱרַע רַק מַה שֶּׁשּׁוֹמְרִין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁמַּקְדִּישׁ עַצְמוֹ מִלְּמַטָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא (ל״ט עַמּוּד א׳) וּמִי שֶׁמִּתְקַדֵּשׁ לְמַטָּה בְּתַכְלִית כֹּחַ הָאֱנוֹשִׁי, כֵּן מְקַדְּשִׁין אוֹתוֹ מִלְּמַעְלָה בְּתַכְלִית כֹּחַ הָאֱלֹהִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ שִׁיעוּר וְנִיצּוֹל גַּם מִטֻּמְאוֹת הַמּוּכְרָחוֹת בְּטֶבַע הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:
records.originEnglish: They asked there, “How did she know?” (Berakhot 10b), for the holiness of the covenant is a private matter and is not visible. One said, “She did not see a fly upon his table.” That is, she recognized that his eating did not arise from the desire of the inclination, which is compared to a fly, as is taught there on 61a. From this she knew that he also maintained the boundary against forbidden sexual relations. Another said, “She spread a linen sheet for him and saw no seminal emission upon it.” Although the strain of travel can sometimes bring about such an emission even in pious people, as is taught in Shabbat 127b, this is something a person cannot prevent through his own effort. He is protected from above according to the extent to which he sanctifies himself below, as is taught in Yoma 39a. Someone who sanctifies himself below to the utmost of human capacity is likewise sanctified from above to the utmost of Divine power, which has no measure, and is saved even from impurities that the nature of this world would otherwise necessitate.
records.themeTitle: Refinement reaches the limits of human control

records.targetHebrew: וּמִטַּעַם זֶה פָּתַח בִּמְדְרַשׁ רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה זוֹ בַּפָּסוּק: "שִׁמְעִי בַת וּרְאִי וְהַטִּי אָזְנֵךְ וְגוֹמֵר", שֶׁהוּא נִדְרָשׁ עַל אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב גַּם בְּמִדְרַשׁ תַּנְחוּמָא; וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צִוָּה לוֹ שֶׁמִּצִּדּוֹ צָרִיךְ שֶׁיְּבָרֵר עַצְמוֹ בְּמִדָּתוֹ וּבְכָל הַמִּדּוֹת, שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע וְיִרְאֶה רַק עֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר לוֹ: "לֶךְ לְךָ" – לְאַתְקָנָא דַּרְגָּא דִילָךְ; וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִבְטִיחוֹ בֶּעָתִיד: "וְאֶעֶשְׂךָ", שֶׁאֲנִי בּוֹרֵא אוֹתְךָ בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הַחֲמִשָּׁה אֵבָרִים גַּם כֵּן בִּרְשׁוּתוֹ, וְהַיְינוּ אַחַר שֶׁיְּבָרֵר אֶת עַצְמוֹ כְּפִי כֹּחוֹ.
records.targetEnglish: For this reason the Midrash Rabbah on this portion opens with the verse, “Listen, daughter, and see, and incline your ear.” It is interpreted as referring to Abraham our father, of blessed memory, as is also taught in the Tanchuma. The blessed God commanded him that, on his own side, he must refine himself in his own quality and in every quality, so that he should hear and see only the service of the blessed God. This is what was said to him: “Go for yourself”—to put your own level right. The blessed God promised him for the future, “And I will make you”: I will create you as a new being, so that the five organs too will be under his control. This comes after he has refined himself according to his capacity.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik gives Abraham’s “new creation” the same sequence as Elisha’s protection: first refinement according to human capacity, then a gift that reaches beyond that capacity. Earlier in the ois, the five organs are identified as the two eyes, two ears, and circumcision. This explains why Yisrael Kedoshim treats the involuntary part of the attainment as sanctification from above, rather than simply more strenuous self-control.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Human refinement followed by a new creation
records.reverseThemeSummary: Abraham is commanded to refine his qualities according to his capacity. The promised new creation then brings even the five organs described earlier in the ois into the service of God.
records.reverseExplanation: Yisrael Kedoshim makes the limit of human effort explicit through Elisha’s bodily purity: some conditions cannot be prevented by choice alone. Its distinction between sanctification below and protection above clarifies why Peri Tzadik describes Abraham’s later attainment as a new creation after his own refinement.

records.originEnglish: They asked there, “How did she know?” (Berakhot 10b), for the holiness of the covenant is a private matter and is not visible. One said, “She did not see a fly upon his table.” That is, she recognized that his eating did not arise from the desire of the inclination, which is compared to a fly, as is taught there on 61a. From this she knew that he also maintained the boundary against forbidden sexual relations. Another said, “She spread a linen sheet for him and saw no seminal emission upon it.” Although the strain of travel can sometimes bring about such an emission even in pious people, as is taught in Shabbat 127b, this is something a person cannot prevent through his own effort. He is protected from above according to the extent to which he sanctifies himself below, as is taught in Yoma 39a. Someone who sanctifies himself below to the utmost of human capacity is likewise sanctified from above to the utmost of Divine power, which has no measure, and is saved even from impurities that the nature of this world would otherwise necessitate.

records.targetEnglish: The meaning is this: in this domain there is an extremely great expansion, forgetfulness, and concealment, to the extent that even a righteous person sometimes fathers a wicked person. The beneficial counsel for a person even here is to diminish and restrain this domain according to his capacity. He can then say, “Go to the Craftsman who made me,” who did not give me greater power. When a person restrains himself according to his capacity, through great labor in service, as far as his reach extends, then in the domain where human power does not reach or rule—as in procreation, which necessarily involves forgetfulness and concealment—he can rely on the plea “Go to the Craftsman who made me.” That is, the blessed God will complete the matter for his good. Consequently this person will see that nothing in the world exists apart from God: every thing has a connection to the blessed God, who created everything, governs everything, and rules everything. The person, on his own side, has no independent power at all.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov explicitly separates restraint within one’s power from the aspects of embodied life that exceed conscious control. Only after the former does he invoke the Creator’s completion of what the creature cannot do. This closely illuminates the structure of Yisrael Kedoshim’s argument about Elisha, while keeping the condition of real human refinement intact.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Doing the available work before entrusting what exceeds it
records.reverseThemeSummary: The covenantal restraint discussed in this ois creates a conscious connection between human action and its source. Where human power ends, the person who has exerted that power can appeal to the Creator’s completion.
records.reverseExplanation: Yisrael Kedoshim supplies a concrete bodily example of Beit Yaakov’s boundary between effort and what exceeds effort. Elisha’s protection from involuntary impurity is described as sanctification from above in response to human sanctification below. This makes clear why the appeal to the Craftsman follows, rather than replaces, the work within one’s capacity.

records.originEnglish: The inquiry into the work of Creation that is entrusted to each person is reflection on the purpose of the creation of the world and of the human being: it was only for His sake. This is the beginning of a person’s awakening. Many ethical works open with this reminder, such as the ethical Sefer HaYashar attributed to Rabbeinu Tam and similar works, to awaken a person to make the effort to improve his deeds on this basis. The goal of the awakening is to recognize that the entire purpose of Creation is to make known the glory of His kingship and the truth of His unity. Israel was chosen to make this known through the Torah and its mitzvot that were given to it; this recognition is the entire purpose of Torah and mitzvot. There is no fixed measure for this reflection, for the Torah did not prescribe how far one must investigate in this contemplation or what form the inquiry must take. Nevertheless, a person must at least set aside a time to reflect on it. The manner of the reflection follows the capacity of his intellect, through his own understanding and through books and scholars.
records.themeTitle: Reflection on Creation should improve the way one lives
records.themeSummary: The inquiry accessible to everyone concerns Creation’s purpose and the recognition of Divine unity. Rav Tzadok makes its practical aim explicit: awakening the effort to improve one’s deeds.
records.targetHebrew: וְהוּא עַד דֻּגְמַת מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְהָיוּ עֵינֶיךָ רֹאוֹת אֶת מוֹרֶיךָ", שֶׁהוּא שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁיִּרְאֶה יִלְמוֹד מִזֶּה אֵיזֶה דָבָר לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁבְּוַדַּאי לֹא לְחִנָּם הֶרְאוּ לוֹ דָּבָר זֶה, רַק כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּלְמוֹד מִזֶּה דֶּרֶךְ ה'; וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁיִּשְׁמַע יִלְמוֹד מִזֶּה לְדַרְכֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: "וְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמַעְנָה דָבָר מֵאַחֲרֶיךָ [לֵאמֹר] זֶה הַדֶּרֶךְ לְכוּ בוֹ", וְהוּא שֶׁיֵּדַע שֶׁלֹּא לְחִנָּם הִמְצִיא לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּשְׁמַע זֶה הַדָּבָר, וּבְוַדַּאי הוּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּלְמוֹד מִזֶּה דֶּרֶךְ ה'. וְזֶה שֶׁאָמְרוּ: "אֵיזֶהוּ חָכָם? הַלּוֹמֵד מִכָּל אָדָם", וְהַיְינוּ מִכָּל מַה שֶּׁיִּשְׁמַע וְיִרְאֶה יִלְמוֹד, אַף שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְכַוֵּין לְלַמְּדוֹ; וְזֶה זָכָה אַחַר הַמִּילָה לִהְיוֹת נַעֲשָׂה בְּרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה, שֶׁעֵינָיו וְאָזְנָיו יִרְאוּ וְיִשְׁמְעוּ רַק דְּבַר מִצְוָה, לִלְמוֹד דֶּרֶךְ ה'.
records.targetEnglish: This corresponds to what is said, “Your eyes shall see your teachers”: from everything one sees, one should learn something for the service of the blessed God. Certainly this sight was not shown to him for nothing, but so that he should learn the way of God from it. Similarly, from what he hears he should learn the ways of service, as it is said, “Your ears shall hear a word behind you, [saying,] ‘This is the way; walk in it.’” He should know that the blessed God did not arrange for him to hear this thing for nothing; it was certainly so that he should learn God’s way from it. This is what they said: “Who is wise? One who learns from every person.” He learns from everything he hears and sees, even when the other person does not intend to teach him. Abraham attained this after circumcision, becoming a new creation whose eyes and ears would see and hear only a matter of mitzvah, learning the way of God.
records.explanation: Peri Tzadik describes a concrete practice for the reflective duty in Sefer HaZikhronot: attend to what is seen and heard as instruction for service. The point of an encounter is not merely to acquire an idea about the world, but to learn a way of serving God from it. This clarifies how contemplation of Creation’s purpose can become the improvement of conduct that Sefer HaZikhronot seeks.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Learning Divine service from what one sees and hears
records.reverseThemeSummary: The refinement of Abraham’s senses means that an encounter becomes instruction in Divine service, even when no one intended to teach. The relevant question is what this particular encounter can teach.
records.reverseExplanation: Sefer HaZikhronot places learning from one’s surroundings within the duty to reflect on Creation’s purpose. It specifies that such reflection is measured by the person’s understanding and should awaken the effort to improve deeds. This explains the practical direction of Peri Tzadik’s repeated phrase “to learn the way of God” from a sight or a word.

records.originEnglish: The inquiry into the work of Creation that is entrusted to each person is reflection on the purpose of the creation of the world and of the human being: it was only for His sake. This is the beginning of a person’s awakening. Many ethical works open with this reminder, such as the ethical Sefer HaYashar attributed to Rabbeinu Tam and similar works, to awaken a person to make the effort to improve his deeds on this basis. The goal of the awakening is to recognize that the entire purpose of Creation is to make known the glory of His kingship and the truth of His unity. Israel was chosen to make this known through the Torah and its mitzvot that were given to it; this recognition is the entire purpose of Torah and mitzvot. There is no fixed measure for this reflection, for the Torah did not prescribe how far one must investigate in this contemplation or what form the inquiry must take. Nevertheless, a person must at least set aside a time to reflect on it. The manner of the reflection follows the capacity of his intellect, through his own understanding and through books and scholars.
records.themeTitle: Reflection on Creation should improve the way one lives
records.themeSummary: The inquiry accessible to everyone concerns Creation’s purpose and the recognition of Divine unity. Rav Tzadok makes its practical aim explicit: awakening the effort to improve one’s deeds.

records.targetHebrew: הָעִנְיָן בָּזֶה: שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר רָאָה שֶׁהֵם מִתְבַּטְּלִים זֶה מִפְּנֵי זֶה, הֵבִין מִזֶּה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא הִסְתִּיר עַצְמוֹ לְגַמְרֵי; לָזֶה הִצִּיב שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם יַכִּירוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ גָּבוֹהַּ עֲלֵיהֶם וּמוֹשֵׁל בָּהֶם וְלֹא יַבִּיטוּ רַק אֵלָיו. וּלְזֶה גַּם כֵּן הֶעֱמִיד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּעוֹלָם בְּכָל דָּבָר זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה. וְכִדְכְתִיב גַּם כֵּן (יְשַׁעְיָהוּ מ, כו): "שְׂאוּ מָרוֹם עֵינֵיכֶם וּרְאוּ מִי בָרָא אֵלֶּה": "אֵלֶּה" הַיְינוּ כָּל הַפְּרָטִים שֶׁהִצִּיב הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּעוֹלָם, וּ"מִי" הוּא אֲתַר דְּקַיְימָא לִשְׁאֵלָה, שֶׁיְּבַקֵּשׁ הָאָדָם לָדַעַת: מִי בָּרָא אֵלֶּה. וּלְזֶה הַמְּכֻוָּון בָּרָא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּל הַפְּרָטִים הַנִּקְרָאִים "אֵלֶּה", וְכִדְאִיתָא בְּהַקְדָּמַת זֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (א עַמּוּד ב) (וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר בְּפָרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית) שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ שֶׁיִּשְׁאֲלוּ הַבְּרוּאִים מִי הוּא הַבּוֹרֵא, וְלָכֵן בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא דְּבָרִים הָפְכִיִּים בָּעוֹלָם.
records.targetEnglish: The meaning is this: when Abraham saw that they give way before one another, he understood that the blessed God had not concealed Himself completely. He had therefore established two opposites, so that through both of them people would recognize that there is One above them who rules them, and would direct their attention only to Him. For this reason the blessed God also established male and female throughout the world. Likewise it is written, “Lift your eyes on high and see: Who created these?” (Isaiah 40:26). “These” means all the particulars that the blessed God established in the world. “Who” is the place that stands open to questioning: a person should seek to know who created these. For this purpose the blessed God created all the particulars called “these.” As is taught in the introduction to the holy Zohar (1b), and as was explained in Bereishit, the blessed God desires that created beings ask who the Creator is. He therefore created opposing things in the world.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov illustrates the inquiry into Creation described in Sefer HaZikhronot. Abraham recognizes limits and oppositions in the visible world and asks about the One who created and governs its particulars. The details of Creation thus become a route to recognition of Divine unity, while the person must actively ask and understand. This is a precise example of the reflection entrusted to each person.

records.reverseThemeTitle: Created particulars invite recognition of their Creator
records.reverseThemeSummary: Abraham learns from the limits and oppositions among created things. Their particulars prompt the question “Who created these?” and call for conscious recognition rather than a substitute that bypasses the person’s own service.
records.reverseExplanation: Sefer HaZikhronot explains the practical purpose of asking “Who created these?”: the recognition of Divine unity should awaken a person to improve his deeds. It also states that the form of the inquiry follows the individual’s capacity, clarifying how the questioning modeled by Abraham can become a task for each reader.
